title: Small but Mighty: SLM Options and Benefits
subtitle: A plain-English guide to Small Language Models, where they fit, and why teams choose them.

intro.title: What Is an SLM?
paragraphs: SLM stands for Small Language Model. Compared to large models, SLMs are usually faster, cheaper, and easier to run in restricted environments.
They are a strong fit when your tasks are focused, your budget matters, or you need lower-latency responses.

items.title: 1) Classification tasks
items.body: Examples: ticket routing, sentiment labels, FAQ tagging.

callout.text: SLMs perform well when labels are clear and domain-specific.

items.title: 2) Structured extraction
items.body: Pull names, dates, IDs, and fields from predictable documents.

code.content:
Input: invoice text
Output: { vendor, invoice_number, due_date, total }

items.title: 3) Internal assistants
items.body: Private Q and A over a known policy set or company handbook.

items.title: Lower cost
items.body: Less compute per request can reduce operating costs.

items.title: Faster responses
items.body: Smaller models often produce replies with lower latency.

items.title: Flexible deployment
items.body: Can be easier to run on edge devices or private infrastructure.

items.title: Focused behavior
items.body: Narrow tasks can yield reliable outcomes with fewer prompts.

items.title: Measure your task
items.body: Define what success means before testing models.

items.title: Run a small benchmark
items.body: Test 20 to 50 real examples and score outputs side by side.

items.title: Keep a fallback
items.body: Use a larger model only when confidence is low.

callout.text: A two-tier setup can save money while keeping quality high for hard cases.

footer.heading: Right-Sized AI Wins
footer.text: The best model is not always the biggest one. It is the one that fits the job.

card.title: Small but Mighty SLM
card.summary: A simple guide to SLM options, ideal use cases, and the benefits of right-sized AI models.
